headline: The Fed held rates. Two of twelve wanted them higher.
summary: The Federal Reserve kept its rate at 3.75% to 4% on Wednesday, less than a week before the midterms. It raised the rate in September for the first time in three years. Ten of twelve voted to hold; Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack wanted a quarter point more. Chair Kevin Warsh said inflation is still too high. The next vote is December 8 and 9.
cover_answer: The price of borrowing money. The Fed left it where it was.
table_question: Should a referee listen to the crowd before making a call?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: Today twelve grown-ups in Washington decided how much it costs to borrow money, the way a shop decides what it charges to rent you a bike for an hour. They said: keep the price the same. Ten of them wanted that, and two wanted it a little higher. Nothing changes at our house, and the grown-ups have it.
5-7.why: Renting a bike is a price they know. Twelve people and a vote is the whole story.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old reasons from what is in front of them, so the script turns an interest rate into a bike rental, a price for borrowing something for a while. The word belongs to the adult for now; the child keeps the picture. Expect "do we borrow money?" Yes, most families do, for the house or the car, and the price stayed the same today.

8-12.script: Prices rose 3.7% in the year to September, up from 2.4% before the Iran war pushed up gas. The Fed's one tool is the interest rate, a thermostat. Turn it up and borrowing costs more, so people spend less and prices cool. It went up in September. Wednesday it stayed put, to see if the room is cooling.
8-12.why: One dial, one chain. Waiting is a choice too.
8-12.why_long: This age is working out cause and effect, so the script runs one chain: gas up, prices up, rate up, spending down. The thermostat is the mechanism, and it carries the hard part, that turning the dial and then waiting is itself a decision. Expect "why not turn it up more?" Two of the twelve wanted to. The other ten want more data first.

13-17.script: Should the Fed raise rates a week before an election? The White House warned against it. Wednesday it held, 10 to 2. Chair Kevin Warsh said politics played no role. Second: Trump is trying to fire Lisa Cook, who voted to raise. Is the Fed independent if the president can fire its members?
13-17.why: No politics, says the chair. A firing is underway. Let them weigh it.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once: the chair says politics played no role, and the president is trying to fire a governor who voted against him. The script hands them both and asks what independence means with a firing underway. Expect "so who's right?" Say you don't know, and that the December vote will tell them something.

5-7.a: The extra you pay back when you borrow money. Like renting a bike: you pay a bit for the time you had it.

8-12.q: Why not just make prices stop going up?
8-12.a: No switch for prices. The Fed's one dial is borrowing cost.

8-12.q: Who were the two who wanted it higher?
8-12.a: Lisa Cook, a Fed governor, and Beth Hammack of the Cleveland Fed.

13-17.a: Warsh says no. The White House had warned against a hike.

13-17.q: Can Trump actually fire Lisa Cook?
13-17.a: He's trying, over mortgage fraud claims. Not settled yet.
